title: Slot-sliced load sweep protocol and repeatability checklist
body:
Purpose:
This doc describes a new harness pattern we experimented with to improve throughput benchmark repeatability: slot-sliced load sweeps. The idea: instead of generating client concurrency as undifferentiated parallel threads, we allocate logical time slots and place arrivals deterministically (with controlled jitter) into those slots. This reduces accidental microburst alignment, exposes scheduling artifacts (slot-leak, slot-drift), and makes ramp/warmup behavior easier to reason about across hosts and repeated runs.

Status/context:
- Fresh experiment; comparing to baseline Poisson and staircase load patterns we already use.
- Primary author: Aisha (serving runtime perf). Collabs: Marco (loadgen), Zoe (observability), Ethan (quant paths).
- Goal: increase run-to-run median/90th stability while still stressing tail/batching interactions.

High-level algorithm (slot-sliced):
1) Choose N logical slots per second (e.g., 10, 50, 100). Each slot is a micro-window where up to S arrivals may be scheduled.
2) Map desired client concurrency Q and arrival rate R into per-slot occupancy targets: target_per_slot = (R / slots_per_sec) rounded as needed.
3) For each slot in the sweep period, sample a deterministic sequence (seeded RNG) that places requests into sub-slot offsets. Offsets are small fractions of the slot (0..slot_width) to test micro-timing.
4) Add configurable jitter jitter_pct to each arrival time to simulate network/clock noise.
5) Sweep across slot density (N) and per-slot occupancy (S) to build a 2D surface: occupancy vs slot density.
6) Record batch sizes, per-request latency histogram, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rates, and request-level traces.

Why this is different/useful:
- Forces repeatable distribution of arrivals while still allowing fine-grained microburst exploration.
- Helps detect scheduling granularity bugs (scheduler assigns work in quanta similar to our slots) or queuing thresholds that appear only when many clients align.
- Easier to compare multi-node runs: align seed and slot map across clients so arrivals are equivalent logically even if physical clocks drift.

Required observability hooks:
- Per-request: arrival_timestamp, enqueued_timestamp, dispatched_timestamp, start_infer_timestamp, first_token_timestamp, end_timestamp, model_variant_id, kernel-path-tag.
- Batch-level: batch_size, input_seq_len_mean, kv_cache_hit_ratio, compile_fallback_flag.
- Host-level: GPU_util_pct, GPU_power_watts, CPU_util, network_qdepth, host_rtt_ms.
- Traces: sampling 1 in 100 requests should include full span with GPU kernel markers.

Sample loadgen config (pseudo):
- run_name: slot-sweep-2025-02
- duration: 20m (5m warmup, 15m steady)
- slots_per_sec: [10, 25, 50, 100] (sweep)
- target_rps: [500, 1000, 2000] (outer sweep)
- seed: 12345678 (aligns slot map across clients)
- jitter_pct: 0.02
- per_slot_limit: 4
- arrival_offset_resolution_ms: 1
- interleaving_mode: host-synced | host-randomized (test both)

Warmup and repeatability rules (checklist):
- Use same seed for slot mapping across runs. Document seed in artifact metadata.
- Run at least 3 independent repeats per point (different seeds for jitter only) and discard the first run if steady-state metrics differ by >10% (indicates thermal/priming variability).
- Warmup window must be long enough to fill KV caches and reach steady GPU clock (empirical: 3–5 minutes for large models). For quantized paths, verify first tokens per-run to detect compile fallbacks.
- SLO/steady-window defined on token throughput and GPU occupancy: only include samples after GPU_util > 60% for >30s unless testing low-occupancy points.
- Ensure node clocks are NTP synced; when running multi-host, capture host_clock_offset in metadata.

Metrics to capture and baseline assertions:
- steady_rps_mean, steady_rps_p5/p50/p95
- latency_p50/p95/p99 (end-to-end and modeling-only)
- tokens_per_second (model-level)
- mean_batch_size and batch_size_distribution
- GPU_utilization_timeweighted_avg
- kv_cache_hit_rate
- failed_requests_count and error categories

Pass/fail quick checks (for automation):
- Repeatability: 3 runs -> coefficient of variation (CoV) of steady_rps_p50 < 0.03 for baseline points. If CoV > 0.05 investigate priming/thermal.
- Batch stability: batch_size_p50 across runs within +/- 0.5.
- No compile_fallbacks in steady window.

Experiment matrix (suggested):
- Axis A (slots_per_sec): 10, 25, 50, 100
- Axis B (target_rps): 250, 500, 1000, 2000
- Axis C (jitter_pct): 0, 0.01, 0.02
- Axis D (interleaving_mode): host-synced, host-randomized
- Repeat each cell 3 times -> prioritize regions where batch size snaps/discontinuous latency jumps observed.

Observational notes / heuristics we found in early runs:
- Very low slot counts (<= 10) tend to create periodic microbursts that interact badly with kernel scheduling, causing periodic 200–400ms spikes in p99 despite p50 being fine.
- High slot density with slight jitter smooths p99 but raises mean batch size, improving tokens/sec but increasing p50. Tradeoffs depend on downstream SLO.
- When slot mapping was not host-synced across clients, we saw artificial smoothing that hid scheduler faults; host-synced mode is better for root-cause repro.
- Compile fallbacks often occur during first 30–90s; capture those traces and exclude runs with fallbacks from final baseline unless investigating cold-compile behavior.

Troubleshooting playbook:
- If run-to-run variance > expected: 1) check host clocks and NTP drift 2) review GPU_FREQ and thermal throttling 3) verify no background jobs on nodes 4) check seed/slot map alignment across clients 5) increase warmup window 6) run single-host isolated test to see if multi-node network/coordination is the cause.
- If batch size distribution shows bi-modal peaks: look for the queuer/dispatcher threshold in the runtime (paging or max-batch timer). Add instrumentation to log dispatcher queue lengths at 100ms resolution.

Artifacts to produce per experiment (minimum):
- metadata.json (flat fields: seed, slots_per_sec, target_rps, host_list, run_id)
- per-request CSV (one row per req with timestamps and tags)
- batch_agg.csv (time-windowed aggregates)
- GPU telemetry dump (sampled at 1s)
- run-level summary TSV with key metrics and pass/fail flags

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Add an agent in loadgen to optionally vary slot width over the sweep so we can simulate long-tailed arrival placements (e.g., some slots span multiple ms).
- Integrate slot-sliced generator into the bench-harness CLI and expose "slot-map" artifact for reproducibility. PR referenced above.
- Flesh out analysis notebook to compute CoV heatmaps across the 2D sweep. Save to confluence.

References and links:
- See related tooling: bench-harness load synthesis library (github PR 188).
- Prior docs: loadgen-replay-checklist, jittered-loadbook (we're intentionally different: deterministic slot mapping vs full randomness).

Summary / recommended next steps:
- Run a full 2D sweep on the quantized 7B path and FP16 13B path across 3 runs each, collect CoV heatmap. Focus investigation on points where p99 jumps > 2x when moving to adjacent slot density.
- If reproducible artifacts found, attach request-level traces and escalate to runtime kernel-selection team with specific batch_size/time-of-day fingerprints.

Bottom line: slot-sliced load sweeps give us a reproducible, debuggable handle on microburst alignment and scheduler interaction. It won't replace Poisson/staircase for all tests, but it's a useful addition to the bench toolkit for root-cause isolation and deterministic comparisons.
